_about: Tier 2 healthcare advertising policies for Clyntique: refined Tier 1 policies based on Yash review feedback (Meta personal health attributes, Google health personalization, Google prescription drug services and restricted drug terms split), plus TikTok healthcare advertising coverage and US FTC regulatory standards. Prepared November 1, 2026. All sources UNVERIFIED and all rule versions DRAFT / UNVERIFIED. Nothing here is approved or active; requires independent verification by Admin A (team@clyntique.demo) and independent approval by Admin B (deepanshisingh1995@gmail.com). Not legal advice.

version.title: Do not assert or imply personal health attributes or medical conditions
version.summary: Meta prohibits ads that assert or imply, directly or through leading questions, that a person has a specific physical or mental health condition, medical diagnosis, or disability, or that the advertiser knows private health details about the viewer or their family. Advertising must focus on describing clinical services, treatments, and general health topics neutrally without targeting or probing the individual viewer's condition.
version.legalExplanation: Meta's Privacy Violations and Personal Attributes advertising standard prohibits asserting or implying personal attributes, including physical or mental health conditions, medical history, and disabilities. The policy explicitly forbids framing that addresses the viewer's health with second-person probing ('Do you have diabetes?', 'Are you suffering from anxiety?'). However, ads that describe health services, medical procedures, or educational health content in the third person ('Treatments available for chronic diabetes', 'Confidential anxiety therapy services') are permitted, provided they do not imply knowledge of the user's personal health status.
version.remediationAction: Rephrase copy from second-person diagnostic inquiries ('Are you struggling with acne?') to objective service descriptions ('Clinical dermatology treatments for acne management'). Describe who the service is for and what care is provided in general terms without addressing the viewer's individual medical history.
applicabilityConditions: Ad runs on Facebook, Instagram, Messenger, or Meta Audience Network.

Ad text, headline, creative imagery, or landing page directly asserts, implies, or asks questions about the viewer's or their family's health condition, medical diagnosis, treatment history, mental health, or physical disability.
exceptions: Public service announcements (PSAs) and public health communications from recognized health authorities that educate the public without asserting or implying that an individual viewer or family member has a health condition.
restrictedClaims: Direct or indirect questions asserting the viewer has a medical diagnosis or condition ('Do you have diabetes?', 'Struggling with depression?')
Copy suggesting or implying the advertiser knows the viewer's or their family member's private health information
Second-person 'you/your' wording tied directly to a physical or mental health attribute, disability, or medical symptom
version.reviewNote: RESEARCHED DRAFT, UNVERIFIED (Nov 1, 2026). Revised from Yash review feedback to provide clear guidance for clinic advertisers and eliminate unsupported restrictions. Verifier questions: (1) verify Meta's latest change log date; (2) confirm clinic guidance examples align with Meta's current enforcement examples; (3) confirm PSA exception wording. Not legal advice.

citations.sectionReference: Privacy Violations and Personal Attributes: Additional guidelines for ads; Physical or mental health and disability
citations.excerpt: Ads must not assert or imply personal attributes. This includes direct or indirect assertions or implications about a person's physical or mental health.

version.title: Restrictions on health-related audience targeting in personalized ads
version.summary: Google restricts personalized advertising for health-related personal hardships and sensitive conditions. Advertisers cannot use advertiser-curated audiences (such as website remarketing lists, Customer Match patient lists, or health-query custom segments) to target users based on physical or mental health conditions, treatments, or procedures. Standard contextual search keyword targeting and Google's predefined non-sensitive audiences remain permitted.
version.legalExplanation: Under Google's Health in Personalized Advertising policy, health is designated a sensitive interest category to protect user privacy. Advertisers are prohibited from building and utilizing first-party or advertiser-managed audiences (including Customer Match email/phone lists, remarketing pixel lists, and custom segments built from sensitive health search queries or URLs) to target people based on medical conditions, prescription treatments, invasive procedures, or cosmetic surgeries. However, Google does NOT prohibit all health advertising: standard contextual keyword targeting on Google Search (e.g. matching queries like 'dermatology clinic Dallas' or 'physical therapy appointment') and Google's predefined, sanitized in-market/affinity audiences are permitted.
version.remediationAction: Remove remarketing tags, Customer Match patient lists, and health-specific custom segments from campaign audience targeting. Switch audience configuration to contextual search keywords, location radius, and language targeting.
applicabilityConditions: Ad runs on Google Ads (Search, Display, YouTube, Gmail, or Discover).

Campaign utilizes audience targeting features (remarketing, Customer Match, custom segments, or user-based lists) linked to sensitive health conditions, medical treatments, clinical procedures, or cosmetic surgery.
exceptions: Contextual search advertising where ads match keywords actively entered by users without audience list retargeting.
Broad predefined Google audience segments (Affinity, In-Market) where Google has excluded sensitive personal health hardship signals.
version.reviewNote: RESEARCHED DRAFT, UNVERIFIED (Nov 1, 2026). Revised from Yash review feedback to clarify restrictions on advertiser-curated audiences vs permitted contextual search and Google predefined audiences. Verifier questions: (1) verify answer 16701855 text on Custom Segments; (2) confirm cosmetic surgery and chronic care scope. Not legal advice.

version.title: Google certification requirements for prescription drug services and telemedicine prescribing
version.summary: Google restricts advertising for services that prescribe, dispense, sell, or facilitate the online fulfillment of prescription drugs. Online pharmacies, digital dispensaries, and telemedicine providers issuing prescription medications must obtain Google Healthcare and Medicines certification and meet jurisdiction-specific accreditation standards (such as LegitScript in the United States). Ordinary physical healthcare clinics providing standard in-person medical consultations without online prescription fulfillment are not subject to pharmacy certification, but any clinic offering remote consultations with prescription services must obtain required telemedicine certifications.
version.legalExplanation: Google's Healthcare and Medicines policy regulates entities involved in the commercial supply chain and remote prescribing of prescription pharmaceuticals. Advertisers operating online prescription drug services, digital pharmacies, or telemedicine platforms that prescribe or dispense medications remotely must apply for and hold Google Healthcare Certification for each targeted country. In the United States, third-party accreditation (such as LegitScript certification for pharmacies or telemedicine) is required before Google grants certification. In the UAE, online pharmacy and telemedicine operations require licensing from the relevant health authority (MOHAP, DHA, or DOH) and Google approval. Standard physical clinics, outpatient practices, and diagnostic centers that provide strictly in-person examinations without remote drug fulfillment or mail-order prescribing are not classified as online pharmacies; however, this exemption applies only to services that do not engage in online prescription dispensing.
version.remediationAction: If the clinic or provider provides telemedicine consultations that issue, fulfill, or deliver prescriptions online, verify whether Google Healthcare Certification and third-party accreditation (such as LegitScript in the US) are required prior to launching ads. If operating an in-person clinical practice, ensure ad copy and landing pages clearly reflect physical consultation services rather than remote prescription dispensing.
applicabilityConditions: Ad runs on Google Ads network.
Advertiser offers, promotes, or facilitates online prescription drug sales, mail-order dispensing, online pharmacy services, or telemedicine prescription issuance.
exceptions: Traditional physical medical practices, outpatient clinics, and diagnostic centers providing strictly in-person examinations without remote drug fulfillment, mail-order prescribing, or digital pharmacy services.
restrictedClaims: Promoting online prescription drug fulfillment, ordering, or mail delivery without verified Google Healthcare Certification
substantiationRequirements: Google Healthcare and Medicines Certification for the advertiser's registered domain in each targeted country
LegitScript or recognized national pharmacy/telemedicine accreditation where required by local country policy (e.g., United States)
version.reviewNote: RESEARCHED DRAFT, UNVERIFIED (Nov 1, 2026). Split from RX-GOOG-HM-01 per review feedback to isolate service provider certification from restricted drug terms. Verifier questions: (1) confirm LegitScript requirements for US telemedicine clinics prescribing remotely; (2) verify UAE health authority documentation requirements for digital health; (3) confirm in-person clinic boundaries. Not legal advice.

version.title: Restrictions on prescription drug brand names, active ingredients, and direct-to-consumer terms in Google Ads
version.summary: Google restricts the use of prescription drug brand names, active pharmaceutical ingredients, and related terms in ad copy, headlines, keywords, and landing pages. Direct-to-Consumer (DTC) advertising of prescription brand names is prohibited in most countries (including the UAE) and strictly limited in the United States, Canada, and New Zealand to certified manufacturers and authorized entities under jurisdiction-specific rules. Ordinary healthcare clinics cannot use prescription drug brand names in consumer-facing ad text or headlines, and must describe services using generic clinical or procedural terms.
version.legalExplanation: Google's Healthcare and Medicines policy enforces strict content and keyword restrictions regarding prescription drug terms, separate from service provider licensing. In most jurisdictions globally (including the UAE), direct-to-consumer promotion of prescription medicines to the public is prohibited by local law and Google policy; ads mentioning prescription brand names will be disapproved. In the United States, direct-to-consumer advertising is permitted only for certified pharmaceutical manufacturers and authorized parties. In Canada, ads may mention prescription brand names only in price-or-name-only formats without claims or indications. For ordinary medical clinics, aesthetic centers, and outpatient providers, mentioning prescription pharmaceutical brand names (e.g. neurotoxins, GLP-1 agonists, prescription dermatologicals) in ad copy, headlines, or targeted keywords triggers policy disapproval or limited delivery, even if the clinic is fully licensed and staffed by certified physicians.
version.remediationAction: Remove prescription drug brand names and active pharmaceutical ingredients from ad headlines, descriptions, and keyword lists. Replace with generic procedural, specialty, or condition descriptions ('cosmetic wrinkle-smoothing treatment' instead of branded neurotoxins; 'clinical weight-management program' instead of branded GLP-1s). Ensure landing pages emphasize medical consultation and clinical evaluation rather than direct drug promotion.
applicabilityConditions: Ad runs on Google Ads (Search, Display, YouTube, or Shopping).
Ad text, headline, targeted keyword list, or landing page contains prescription drug brand names, active pharmaceutical ingredients, or references to prescription-only medications.
exceptions: Certified pharmaceutical manufacturers holding valid Google prescription drug advertising certification in jurisdictions where direct-to-consumer advertising is legally permitted (such as the United States).
restrictedClaims: Prescription drug brand names or active pharmaceutical ingredients in ad headlines, ad copy, or display URLs without manufacturer certification
Bidding on prescription drug terms as search keywords in countries prohibiting direct-to-consumer prescription drug marketing (including the UAE)
Landing pages promoting direct consumer purchase of prescription-only medicines
substantiationRequirements: Google Healthcare Certification authorizing prescription drug term promotion for the specific targeted jurisdiction (manufacturers only)
version.reviewNote: RESEARCHED DRAFT, UNVERIFIED (Nov 1, 2026). Split from RX-GOOG-HM-01 per review feedback to isolate prescription drug terms from provider licensing. Verifier questions: (1) review US policy for clinic landing-page mentions vs ad copy headlines/text; (2) confirm UAE statutory prohibition on DTC prescription terms; (3) verify Canada price/name exception boundaries. Not legal advice.

version.title: TikTok restrictions on misleading medical claims, absolute cure guarantees, and before/after comparisons
version.summary: TikTok prohibits advertisements that make false, exaggerated, or misleading medical claims, promise guaranteed health outcomes, or feature manipulated or unrepresentative before-and-after imagery. Mandatory 18+ age restrictions specifically apply to weight management, dieting, and fasting creatives. Advertisers must avoid absolute treatment promises, rapid relief guarantees, or body-shaming depictions.
version.legalExplanation: TikTok's Advertising Policies on Misleading and False Content and Exaggerated Claims prohibit ads that promise unrealistic results or make absolute claims regarding health, wellness, and medical efficacy. Disallowed content includes claiming a product cures incurable medical conditions (e.g. cancer, diabetes), guaranteeing specific outcomes ('100% cure', 'relieves pain instantly'), and utilizing before-and-after comparisons that convey a distorted or unachievable result. Under TikTok's Weight Management policies, ads promoting weight management, fasting, or body sculpting must be targeted to users aged 18 and older, and cannot promote rapid or unhealthy weight reduction or negative body self-image. General healthcare services may be subject to different regional requirements, which must be verified per market.
version.remediationAction: Remove absolute promises, guaranteed timelines, and exaggerated efficacy assertions from copy and video scripts. Eliminate dramatic or manipulated before-and-after visual comparisons. For weight management or body contouring campaigns, apply 18+ audience targeting. Frame health services around professional consultations, clinical safety, and individualized care.
applicabilityConditions: Ad runs on TikTok (In-Feed Ads, TopView, Spark Ads, or branded formats).
Creative copy, voiceover, video imagery, or landing page features medical claims, health treatment outcomes, before-and-after visual comparisons, or weight management assertions.
restrictedClaims: Guaranteed medical cures, 100% success claims, or absolute promises of health restoration
Claims of instant or rapid relief ('cures in 24 hours', 'instant weight loss')
Curing or preventing medically incurable chronic diseases
Manipulated, dramatic, or unrepresentative before-and-after visual comparisons
substantiationRequirements: Competent scientific documentation verifying any objective clinical efficacy statement made in the advertisement
version.reviewNote: RESEARCHED DRAFT, UNVERIFIED (Nov 1, 2026). Researched from TikTok Advertising Policies (Misleading Content & Weight Management). Verifier questions: (1) verify TikTok help article 10002871 misleading content sections; (2) confirm before-and-after tolerances for non-surgical aesthetic clinics; (3) confirm market-specific weight management age-gating rules. Not legal advice.

version.title: TikTok healthcare and pharmaceuticals industry entry and market-specific qualification requirements
version.summary: TikTok regulates healthcare and pharmaceutical advertising through category-specific Industry Entry rules that vary by country. Prescription medicines are generally prohibited from standard self-serve advertising. Permitted categories (such as over-the-counter medicines, medical devices, and clinic services) require verified regulatory documentation, with age-gating (18+) required for specific restricted categories like weight management or cosmetic procedures. In regulated markets like the UAE, local health authority approvals and advertising documentation are required prior to onboarding, subject to regional verification.
version.legalExplanation: Under TikTok's Industry Entry standards for Healthcare and Pharmaceuticals (Help Article 10003058), advertising health-related products and services is governed by a detailed market-by-market matrix. Promotion of prescription-only medicines is prohibited on standard self-serve ad accounts in most jurisdictions, though managed accounts or disease awareness campaigns may be subject to specific exceptions in select markets. Permitted health categories—including over-the-counter (OTC) medicines, medical devices, and outpatient clinics—require submission of official business and regulatory documentation. Age targeting restrictions vary: while weight management and certain cosmetic procedures require mandatory 18+ targeting, general health services follow market-specific rules. In the UAE, healthcare advertising requires appropriate regulatory authorizations (such as MOHAP, DHA, or DOH facility licensing and advertising permits), but specific TikTok MENA regional onboarding requirements must be confirmed against the live country table.
version.remediationAction: Check TikTok's country-specific industry entry table for the targeted market before campaign setup. Prepare valid clinic facility licenses and practitioner credentials. Where promoting weight management, cosmetic procedures, or restricted health categories, ensure 18+ age targeting is configured. Remove direct promotion of prescription-only drugs from standard ad accounts.
applicabilityConditions: Ad runs on TikTok Ads Manager targeting any market.
Advertiser operates within the Healthcare, Medical, Pharmaceutical, Dental, or Medical Aesthetics industries.
restrictedClaims: Promotion of prescription-only medicines on standard self-serve ad accounts without authorized platform approval
Serving restricted health categories (such as weight management or cosmetic surgery) to audiences under 18 years old
Running healthcare advertising in regulated markets without submitting required local health authority documentation
substantiationRequirements: Valid healthcare facility operating license or physician credential from the jurisdiction of operation
Market-specific advertising authorization or regulatory documentation where required by local health authorities (e.g. UAE)
Audience targeting documentation verifying appropriate age gating for restricted categories (e.g. 18+ for weight management)

Not legal advice.

version.title: FTC competent and reliable scientific evidence standard for healthcare and wellness claims
version.summary: Under Section 5 of the FTC Act and the FTC Health Products Compliance Guidance, all objective health, wellness, and medical efficacy claims must be substantiated by competent and reliable scientific evidence (CARSE) prior to dissemination. The required level and type of evidence are context-dependent and determined by the Pfizer factors (including claim type, product nature, and consensus of qualified experts in the field). While disease treatment, cure, or serious prevention claims generally require well-controlled clinical testing, the FTC does not mandate randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled RCTs for all health claims across the board.
version.legalExplanation: The Federal Trade Commission enforces substantiation standards under Sections 5 and 12 of the FTC Act (15 U.S.C. §§ 45, 52). Under the FTC's Health Products Compliance Guidance (December 2022), advertisers must possess a 'reasonable basis' consisting of competent and reliable scientific evidence (CARSE) before making any objective claim regarding health benefits, safety, or efficacy. CARSE is defined as tests, analyses, research, or studies conducted and evaluated in an objective manner by qualified persons, using procedures generally accepted in the profession to yield accurate and reliable results. Under established FTC doctrine (the Pfizer factors), there is no single fixed formula for substantiation; the requisite amount and type of evidence depend on the claim, the product, the consequences of a false claim, and what experts in the relevant scientific discipline consider reasonable. While claims regarding serious diseases or clinical cures typically require well-controlled human clinical trials, the FTC does not impose a rigid blanket requirement that every objective health claim must have randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled RCTs. Uncontrolled consumer surveys, animal studies alone, or unverified clinician impressions do not substitute for human testing where human evidence is scientifically necessary.
version.remediationAction: Review all healthcare and wellness claims against the underlying scientific substantiation in possession prior to campaign launch. Ensure claims do not exceed the scope or strength of what qualified scientific experts in the field consider established. Clearly qualify any preliminary research or disclose study limitations if claims are not supported by definitive human clinical consensus.
applicabilityConditions: Ad targets consumers in the United States across any medium (digital, social, search, print, broadcast, or landing page).
Creative makes express or implied claims regarding health benefits, disease prevention, medical treatment, pain reduction, anti-aging efficacy, or therapeutic outcomes.
restrictedClaims: Health, therapeutic, or medical efficacy claims made without prior possession of competent and reliable scientific evidence
Express or implied claims of clinical proof or established health benefits that exceed the scientific consensus of supporting studies
Extrapolating preliminary in vitro or animal findings to claim proven human health benefits when human clinical data is required by experts
Relying on subjective consumer testimonials or anecdotal clinician reports to substantiate objective health claims
substantiationRequirements: Competent and reliable scientific evidence evaluated by qualified experts, with study design, methodology, sample size, and duration appropriate for the specific claim and product
version.reviewNote: RESEARCHED DRAFT, UNVERIFIED (Nov 1, 2026). Researched from FTC Health Products Compliance Guidance (Dec 2022). Statutory regulation, distinct from platform policy. Verifier questions: (1) verify Pfizer factors application to clinic and wellness services; (2) verify when human clinical trials vs other recognized scientific methodologies satisfy CARSE; (3) confirm standards for qualifying preliminary health research. Not legal advice.

version.title: FTC requirements for healthcare testimonials, typicality disclosures, and material connections
version.summary: Under FTC Endorsement Guides (16 CFR Part 255), consumer testimonials depicting health or medical outcomes must reflect honest experiences and representative results. If an endorser's experience is not generally achievable, the advertiser must clearly and conspicuously disclose the generally expected performance; disclaimers like 'results may vary' are legally insufficient. Furthermore, any material connection between an endorser and the advertiser (such as payment, free treatment, discounts, or employment) must be clearly and conspicuously disclosed.
version.legalExplanation: Under 16 CFR Part 255 (Guides Concerning the Use of Endorsements and Testimonials in Advertising), consumer and expert endorsements in health advertising are strictly regulated. Pursuant to 16 CFR § 255.2, an advertisement utilizing a consumer testimonial (e.g. extraordinary patient weight loss, rapid skin restoration, or dramatic pain elimination) implies that the experience is representative of what consumers will generally achieve. If the advertiser lacks substantiation that such results are typical, the ad must clearly and conspicuously disclose the generally expected results in the depicted circumstances. Vague, boilerplate disclaimers such as 'Results not typical' or 'Results may vary' do not cure deception. Pursuant to 16 CFR § 255.5, if there exists a material connection between the endorser and the advertiser that the audience would not reasonably expect—including monetary compensation, free clinical procedures, product gifts, employee status, or familial relationships—such connection must be clearly and prominently disclosed in immediate visual or auditory proximity to the endorsement (e.g. '#PaidAd', 'Complimentary treatment provided').
version.remediationAction: If featuring patient testimonials with exceptional results, add a clear and conspicuous disclosure stating the generally expected performance based on clinical substantiation. If the patient, influencer, or practitioner received compensation, free treatment, or has an affiliation with the clinic, ensure an unambiguous disclosure of material connection is visibly integrated into the creative before the viewer engages.
applicabilityConditions: Ad targets consumers in the United States across any medium (video, image, text, influencer post, or landing page).
Creative features consumer reviews, patient testimonials, influencer endorsements, clinician recommendations, or user-generated experience stories.
restrictedClaims: Patient testimonials presenting non-typical health outcomes without clear and conspicuous disclosure of generally expected results
Relying on vague disclaimers such as 'Results may vary' or 'Results not typical' to defend atypical testimonials
Endorsements where compensation, free procedures, or material connections are hidden, omitted, or buried behind links or obscure hashtags
substantiationRequirements: Scientific substantiation demonstrating that consumer experiences depicted in testimonials represent generally expected performance, or documented evidence supporting the disclosed typical results
Written record of material connection disclosures for all sponsored patients, influencers, and brand advocates
